Hi Alex / Sophie,

Great to meet you both on the call today — thanks for the time. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our side so we keep momentum: 

Summary of what we heard:
- You run in AWS on EKS with downstream services that require private egress and strict IP controls.
- Compliance wants mTLS for any private endpoints and an audit trail for network connections.
- Ideally you’d prefer VPC endpoints / PrivateLink over opening broad internet egress, but you also have NAT gateways for occasional external traffic.
- You’re interested in embeddings and a re-ranker pipeline; want assurance that traffic between your VPC and Redwood is private and authenticated.

Action items / next steps:
1) Technical deep dive w/ our solutions engineering to go over VPC endpoints, IP allowlist, DNS, and mTLS requirements — estimate ~45–60m. Can you share preferred times next week?
2) You to share a redacted network diagram and the security contact for the compliance questionnaire.
3) We’ll send a prescriptive IP allowlist and RN (recommended) connection patterns for SDK auth (OIDC/service-account vs mTLS) and routing for structured output/tool-calling + embeddings.
4) I'll attach a short quickstart and an integration outline so your infra team can pre-read.

Attaching: redwood_vpc_quickstart.pdf, redwood_integration_outline.docx

If this looks right I’ll loop in Jonas (SE) and Lauren (solutions lead) to schedule the deep-dive.

Best,

Thanks Marissa — that summary is spot on. A few clarifications from our infra/security side: 

- We run in AWS (us-west-2) on EKS with private subnets and NAT gateways for outbound internet. We'd prefer PrivateLink / VPC endpoints for long-lived production traffic; ephemeral model downloads could be allowed via our NAT.
- Compliance requires mTLS to any production vendor endpoint. We have an internal PKI and can provision client certs if needed.
- For DNS: internal services resolve internal names; if Redwood needs to access internal-only hostnames we'd need either inbound connectivity (VPN/Transit Gateway) or DNS forwarding.
- We will redact and share a network diagram — attaching a first draft here: internal_network_diag.png.

Questions for Redwood: 
1) Do you publish a stable set of IP ranges we can allowlist, or do you recommend PrivateLink?
2) For mTLS, do you support client certificates + CA rotation?
3) How does SDK auth work for server-to-server calls? We prefer short-lived tokens or OIDC if possible.

We can meet Wed or Thu next week after 10am PT. Sophie and I will be on the call; Sophie is our security lead.

Thanks,

Hi Alex / Sophie / Marissa,

Thanks for looping me in — happy to run the deep-dive. A few technical notes in advance so your infra team has context: 

1) Connectivity options and our recommendations:
- PrivateLink / VPC endpoints: recommended for production traffic where you want stable, private connectivity. We can support Interface VPC Endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for our hosted endpoints or a Private deployment inside your VPC.
- IP allowlist: for hosted endpoints we publish a small set of egress IP ranges (examples below) but these can change — we provide SFDC/HubSpot notifications and an API endpoint to fetch current ranges. For strict compliance, PrivateLink is best.

Example (sample only):
- Hosted API public egress: 34.216.10.0/24, 54.187.33.0/24
- Dedicated edge IPs (region us-west-2): 3.120.45.0/26, 3.120.46.0/26

2) mTLS & certs:
- We support mutual TLS on Dedicated and Private deployments. Client certs can be rotated; our deployment supports short-lived certs (recommended) and automatic CA rollover. We can accept either your internal CA or issue certs from our CA depending on preference.

3) SDK auth patterns:
- Server-to-server: OIDC-based short-lived tokens (recommended) or service account API keys with rotation.
- For Private deployments we also support subject-bound certs and workload identities.

4) DNS / egress patterns:
- For PrivateLink, DNS entries are created in your account (private hosted zone) to resolve vendor endpoints to the interface endpoint.
- If you need outbound DNS to resolve internal-only hostnames, we recommend forwarding via a shared resolver or conditional forwarding to your internal DNS.

Attached: network_config_examples.yaml (examples for iptables, route tables, and sample security group rules).

We’ll bring these specifics to the call and can walk through a packet-flow diagram showing where embeddings/requests flow (client -> Redwood endpoint -> embeddings/reranker -> back to client).

Proposed times noted — Wed 11am PT works for me.

Cheers,
Jonas Weber
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
